content: 1. Routine screening for Hepatitis C Virus (HCV) is almost certainly cost-effective in populations with typical prevalence estimates of 40%, and even more so in cohorts where prevalence reaches as high as 75%. This is particularly true when considering the HCV cascade of care, especially for individuals with recent or ongoing drug use. 2. Men who have sex with men (MSM), particularly those who are HIV-positive, are at an increased risk of HCV infection. Preliminary studies suggest that core-antigen testing may be a cost-effective approach for this population, provided there is appropriate linkage to effective therapy and retention in care. However, these studies do not fully account for reductions in secondary transmission or the potential for reinfection in high-risk groups. 3. Prisons often have a high prevalence of HCV due to the significant number of individuals who inject drugs within these settings. While HCV testing in prisons can be cost-effective, challenges include the high cost of new HCV treatments and limited access to these therapies for incarcerated individuals. Targeted screening of prisoners with a history of injection drug use improves cost-effectiveness compared to universal screening of all prisoners. 4. Nearly all HCV care guidelines recommend screening at the time of enrollment in care. However, there is a lack of cost-effectiveness analyses specifically addressing the value of HCV testing at this stage. Given the high prevalence of HCV in HIV-infected individuals, the rapid progression of fibrosis in HIV/HCV co-infected patients, and the effectiveness of new therapies, testing for HCV at enrollment in care is almost certainly cost-effective. 5. There is insufficient evidence to determine the cost-effectiveness of routine HCV testing among sex workers. Many sex workers are also people who inject drugs (PWID) or use non-injection drugs, which likely increases the prevalence of HCV in this group. It remains unclear whether routine screening of all sex workers is cost-effective compared to targeted testing of those with a history of injection drug use. 6. Birth-cohort testing, which targets easily identifiable demographic groups with high HCV prevalence (e.g., individuals born during a specific time period), is likely cost-effective. Studies in the United States and Portugal have demonstrated that this approach is cost-effective, though the specific cohorts to test may vary based on local HCV epidemiology. 7. Routine testing of the general population, without identifying high-risk behaviors or demographics, is not currently recommended in any jurisdiction. Studies from high-income countries (HICs) like the US and UK suggest that such an approach is not cost-effective. Universal testing often results in worse outcomes and higher costs compared to targeted approaches like birth-cohort testing. 8. The cost-effectiveness of HCV testing depends on several factors, including the cost of testing itself, the prevalence of HCV in the population, and the availability of effective therapies. Over-targeting testing to only the highest-risk groups can lead to under-testing due to stigma and underreporting of high-risk behaviors. Conversely, broad testing efforts may dilute resources and fail to identify cases efficiently. 9. The efficacy of HCV therapy significantly impacts the cost-effectiveness of testing. If effective treatment is unavailable or inaccessible, the incremental cost-effectiveness ratio of screening increases. Similarly, assumptions about the HCV cascade of care, including linkage to care and retention, play a critical role in determining cost-effectiveness. 10. Faster rates of fibrosis progression make HCV testing more cost-effective, as a larger proportion of the population will experience complications of HCV. Conversely, slower progression rates reduce the immediate benefits of testing, as many patients may never develop severe liver disease. 11. Accurate epidemiological data is essential to inform decisions about HCV testing strategies. Further research is needed to compare the cost-effectiveness of targeted, birth-cohort, and routine testing approaches, particularly in lowand middle-income countries (LMICs). Implementation research is also necessary to evaluate the ability of providers to identify and test high-risk patients effectively. 12. Testing in high-risk groups such as PWID, MSM, prisoners, HIV-infected individuals, and commercial sex workers is likely cost-effective. In settings with a high prevalence of high-risk patients, testing is almost certainly cost-effective, provided there is adequate follow-up after diagnosis. 13. Outside of high-risk groups, the best testing approach depends on a country’s unique HCV epidemiology. Birth-cohort testing is likely cost-effective in most settings, as it targets easily identifiable groups without stigma. However, routine testing of the entire population carries risks, particularly in settings where the HCV epidemic is concentrated in specific age or risk groups.
